prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Quiet, And, Were

outputs.L1:
In your arms was still delight,  
Quiet as a street at night;  
And thoughts of you, I do remember,  
Were green leaves in a darkened chamber,  
Were dark clouds in a moonless sky.  

Love, in you, went passing by,  
Penetrative, remote, and rare,  
Like a bird in the wide air;  
And, as the bird, it left no trace  
In the heaven of your face.  

In your stupidity I found  
The sweet hush after a sweet sound.  
All about you was the light  
That dims the greying end of night;  
Desire was the unrisen sun,  
Joy the day not yet begun,  
With tree whispering to tree,  
Without wind, quietly.  

Wisdom slept within your hair,  
And Long-Suffering was there;  
And, in the flowing of your dress,  
Undiscerning Tenderness.  

And when you thought, it seemed to me,  
Infinitely, and like a sea,  
About the slight world you had known  
Your vast unconsciousness was thrown . . .  

O haven without wave or tide!  
Silence, in which all songs have died!  
Holy book, where hearts are still!  
And home at length under the hill!  
O mother quiet, breasts of peace,  
Where love itself would faint and cease!  

O infinite deep I never knew,  
I would come back, come back to you,  
Find you, as a pool unstirred,  
Kneel down by you, and never a word,  
Lay my head, and nothing said,  
In your hands, ungarlanded;  
And a long watch you would keep;  
And I should sleep, and I should sleep!
outputs.L2:
In your embrace there was still happiness,  
Silent like a road after dark.  
I remember that my thoughts of you  
Were like fresh leaves inside a shadowed room,  
Like heavy clouds beneath a sky with no moon.  

Love, within you, seemed to drift past—  
Deep-reaching, distant, and uncommon—  
Like a bird moving through open air;  
And, just like that bird, it left no mark  
Across the sky of your face.  

In your foolishness, I discovered  
The gentle quiet that follows a lovely sound.  
Everything around you held the glow  
That softens the grey close of night.  
Longing was like the sun before it rose,  
Happiness like the day before it began,  
While trees seemed to murmur to one another  
Without any wind, in perfect stillness.  

Wisdom rested hidden in your hair,  
And patience in suffering was present too;  
And in the motion of your dress  
There was a tender kindness that did not judge.  

Whenever you were thinking, it appeared to me  
As though, endlessly and like the sea,  
Your immense unknowing spread itself  
Over the small world you had experienced.  

O shelter untouched by wave or tide!  
O quiet where every song has ended!  
O sacred volume in which hearts grow calm!  
O final home beneath the hill!  
O peaceful mother, with breasts of rest,  
Where even love would weaken and fall still!  

O boundless depth I never understood,  
I would return, return to you—  
Find you like water lying perfectly calm,  
Kneel beside you without speaking,  
Lay down my head, saying nothing,  
In your bare, unadorned hands.  
You would keep a long vigil,  
And I would sleep, and sleep.
outputs.L3:
The speaker remembers the beloved as a quiet and distant presence, one whose love is gentle rather than forceful. This love is not dramatic or openly declared; instead, it is subtle, fleeting, and almost hidden. The beloved seems remote, as though separated from the speaker by time, memory, or an emotional distance that cannot be crossed directly. Yet this distance does not diminish the beloved’s power. On the contrary, it makes the memory feel more delicate and sacred, like something glimpsed only briefly but never forgotten.

The beloved is described through images of stillness, darkness, dawn, and the natural world. These images create an atmosphere of peace and mystery. Darkness suggests depth, silence, and concealment, while dawn hints at renewal, softness, and the beginning of light. Nature adds to this sense of calm, making the beloved seem less like an ordinary person and more like a quiet force within the world. The beloved’s presence is therefore both comforting and mysterious: peaceful enough to soothe the speaker, yet distant enough to remain unknowable.

The speaker also associates the beloved with innocence and unconscious wisdom. The beloved does not appear to possess knowledge in an intellectual or deliberate way, but rather a deeper, instinctive understanding. This wisdom is gentle and unspoken, joined with tenderness and patience. There is also a sense of long-suffering calm, as if the beloved has endured sorrow without bitterness or complaint. This makes the beloved seem morally and emotionally pure, a figure of quiet strength whose power lies in endurance, compassion, and silence.

As the memory develops, the beloved becomes more than a personal figure. The beloved turns into a symbol of refuge, silence, and rest. In this presence, the speaker imagines an escape from desire, conflict, and weariness. All striving can come to an end there; all pain and longing can be stilled. The beloved represents a place or state of being where the restless self no longer needs to struggle. This refuge is not active or passionate, but passive, calm, and deeply consoling.

Ultimately, the speaker longs to return to this peaceful presence. The desire is not simply to reunite with the beloved, but to surrender completely into the comfort the beloved represents. The speaker wishes to abandon speech, effort, and conscious thought, entering instead into silence, rest, and sleep. This longing suggests a deep need for release: release from suffering, from desire, and from the burden of wakeful awareness. In the end, the beloved becomes the image of perfect peace, a wordless shelter into which the speaker yearns to disappear.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker who longs not for dramatic passion or spoken affection, but for the beloved’s quiet, unconscious presence. Its imagery is hushed and dreamlike, filled with night, natural beauty, silence, and rest. Rather than imagining love as movement, conversation, or possession, the speaker imagines it as stillness: the beloved asleep, unaware, and peaceful. This unconscious presence becomes deeply meaningful because it offers the speaker a sense of calm that ordinary waking life cannot provide.

Throughout the poem, nature helps create an atmosphere of softness and retreat. Images of darkness, sleep, and quiet suggest a world removed from noise, struggle, and restless desire. The beloved seems almost merged with this peaceful landscape, becoming part of the night’s sheltering silence. In this setting, love is not expressed through action but through nearness and surrender. The speaker’s yearning is therefore both romantic and spiritual: the beloved represents not only personal affection, but also escape from pain, thought, and the burden of self-awareness.

At the heart of the poem is a desire for refuge. The speaker appears weary of longing, suffering, and the ceaseless activity of the mind. In the beloved’s stillness, the speaker finds an image of release—a state in which desire is quieted and sorrow is suspended. This gives the poem a tone that is tender but also melancholy, since the peace the speaker seeks resembles oblivion as much as happiness. Love is imagined as a place where consciousness can finally rest.

By associating the beloved with sleep, silence, and natural calm, the poem suggests that the deepest form of love may not be possession or fulfillment, but the relief of being freed from oneself. The beloved’s quiet presence becomes a sanctuary from the pressures of thought and feeling. In this way, the poem transforms longing into a meditation on peace: it shows how love can become a desire for stillness, and how oblivion, when touched by tenderness, can seem like the most profound comfort.

The village was **quiet**, resting under a pale evening sky. The streets, once filled with footsteps and voices, **were** now empty, as if everyone had agreed to let the night arrive in peace. A soft wind moved through the trees, **and** the only sound was the gentle rustle of leaves.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholy early 20th-century romantic poem in the style of Rupert Brooke, full of quiet imagery, longing, sleep, silence, and idealized love.
counterfactuals.output:
**After the Lamps Are Out**

When all the lamps are out, and streets lie still,  
And rain is whispering along the pane,  
I think your name across the sleeping hill,  
And hear the dark reply with it again.  

The little wind goes barefoot through the grass;  
The moon leans pale above the orchard bars;  
And one by one, as drowsy hours pass,  
The night puts out her trembling store of stars.  

O love, not mine except in dreams and prayer,  
How far you seem, how near your shadow lies—  
A flower shut softly in the midnight air,  
A light remembered under other skies.  

If I might come, when all the world is deep  
In that still country where the tired find peace,  
And touch your hand, and watch you turn in sleep,  
And feel the aching of the heart’s release—  

Then I should ask no dawn, no answered word,  
No kiss to trouble your untroubled breath;  
Only to know my longing had been heard  
In the white silence at the edge of death.  

For love is gentlest where it cannot stay,  
And purest when it has no hope to keep;  
A star that burns beyond the reach of day,  
A face beloved, and hidden now in sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a free-verse/literary poem about returning to a peaceful lover or motherly figure, using moonless skies, birds, dawn, trees, and the desire to sleep forever.
counterfactuals.output:
I come back by the road with no moon,  
the sky a dark bowl rinsed clean of stars,  
and all the fields holding their breath.

Far off, the trees know me.  
They lift their quiet hands,  
black branches combing the wind  
as if to smooth my hair before I arrive.

No lamp is needed.  
Your silence is a house I remember.  
Your arms, whether lover’s or mother’s,  
open like the first warmth  
inside bread, inside earth,  
inside the animal that has run too long.

All night the birds are hidden,  
folded into leaves, dreaming small dawns.  
I envy them—  
their certain nests,  
their faith in morning.

When the east begins  
to loosen its pale thread,  
one bird speaks, then another,  
and the whole world is gently persuaded  
to continue.

But I am tired  
of being persuaded.

Let me lay my head  
where your heartbeat makes a shore.  
Let the trees stand guard.  
Let the birds carry the morning  
over the roofs without me.

If sleep must come,  
let it be here—  
not as an ending,  
but as water returning to water,  
as shadow resting under shadow,  
as a child held so completely  
there is no need to wake  
and ask to be loved.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Georgian-era love poem with archaic diction and mystical imagery, beginning with “In your arms was still delight” and ending with “And I should sleep, and I should sleep!”
counterfactuals.output:
In your arms was still delight,  
As moon-dew on the asphodel;  
Thy whisper, through the folds of night,  
Was like a far-off vesper bell.  

O thou, whose eyes did seem to keep  
Twin stars from Eden’s hidden deep,  
Bend o’er my soul thy tender spell,  
And bid its weary shadows sleep.  

For round thy brow the seraphs wove  
Pale wreaths of fire and amaranth;  
And all the wandering winds of love  
Grew faint along thy fragrant path.  

Ah, take me where the dusk is sweet,  
Where dream and death together meet;  
There let thy heart my vigil keep,  
And I should sleep, and I should sleep!
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a solemn lyric poem about finding rest in a beloved’s unconscious serenity, with themes of tenderness, silence, deathlike peace, and spiritual homecoming.
counterfactuals.output:
**At Your Sleeping Side**

I found you where the lamplight thinned,  
beyond the reach of waking care,  
your breath a tide that had not sinned,  
your hands unburdened in the air.

No word remained for me to say.  
The room had entered holy ground.  
All clocks stood still, or turned away,  
ashamed to trouble such a sound.

How gently death had lent its face—  
not to possess you, but to bless;  
a pale rehearsal of the place  
where grief is changed to quietness.

I watched the dark forgive your brow,  
the world withdraw its iron claim,  
and felt my wandering spirit bow  
before the softness of your name.

O love, in sleep you seemed to be  
already past all fear and foam,  
a shore beyond the mortal sea,  
a window lit inside my home.

So let me rest where you are still,  
beside that peace I cannot keep;  
my heart, long exiled by its will,  
comes home to God when you asleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Reproduce the poem “The Great Lover” or a similar Rupert Brooke-style passage about love, stupidity, quietness, and sleep.
counterfactuals.output:
Here’s an original Rupert Brooke–style passage on love, stupidity, quietness, and sleep:

I have loved foolishly the foolish things—  
The lamplight trembling on a rainy pane,  
The small, absurd contentment evening brings,  
A hand remembered, and remembered pain.  

I have been stupid with the stars, and smiled  
At solemn moons as though they understood;  
Called every silence holy, and beguiled  
My heart with dreams, because the dreams were good.  

And I have loved the quiet: rooms at rest,  
Books shut like sleeping birds, the drowsy fire,  
The hour when thought lies down within the breast  
And all the world forgets its old desire.  

O love, O idiocy sweet and deep,  
To praise what passes, knowing it must pass—  
To kiss the dark, and call the darkness sleep,  
And find heaven folded in the grass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
